newsitem.title: USA: Issuers say Moody's new ratings to include GOs.
newsitem.headline: Issuers say Moody's new ratings to include GOs.

text.p: Moody's Investors Service's new rating designations will be expanded to general obligation debt, according to some municipal bond issuers.

The rating designations, which add the numerical modifiers of "2" and "3" to Moody's ratings of B and above, have already been implemented for health care, higher education, and not-for-profit issuers, and most recently for state revolving fund programs.
Issuers said that Moody's officials have told them the expanded bond rating scale will be applied to GO debt sometime in the future.
Herb Kruse, Ohio's debt coordinator, said he was told that Moody's planned to phase in the plan to include GO and state lease debt.

Frank Hoadley, Wisconsin's capital finance director, said a Moody's official said at a recent Council of Infrastructure Financing Authorities meeting that the expansion to GO's would come fairly soon.

Fran Lazerson, a spokeswoman for Moody's, would not specifically confirm that plans are in the works to include GO bonds. However, she did say that Moody's "will definitely expand the rating scale to other sectors as investors call for it."
"We're reviewing the expansion of our rating categories into other areas of public finance," she said.
The move, amid other changes at Moody's including the loss or reassignment of some rating analysts, is raising concerns among issuers.
"If I was in charge of a big mutual fund I'd be kind of leery of the rating," Kruse said. "It's going to be a problem for awhile until it shakes out."
Kruse's comments came on the heels of well-publicized remarks by Hoadley last week.
On Monday, Hoadley said that he was concerned about the expanded rating scale because of the "uncertainty" it creates.
"The fact of the matter is there are a lot of changes going on at Moody's and a lot of people are concerned about it and we're concerned about it," he said.
In addition to the expansion of the rating scale, another concern cited by Hoadley was the change in analysts that has resulted from an ongoing reorganization at Moody's.
Both he and Kruse acknowledged that analysts who have worked on their states have left Moody's or been reassigned to other departments.

Lazerson said that Moody's does move mid-level managers around to give them a "greater depth and breath" of experience. However, she pointed out that most of the senior analysts at Moody's have not changed.
Hoadley said that Wisconsin is not talking about dropping its Moody's rating.
However, he said a Moody's rating may not be necessary in some cases to achieve the same pricing effect.
"There is ample evidence that you can sell particularly a revenue bond credit without a Moody's rating and not suffer any price differential," Hoadley said.
He said he based that statement on price comparisons "provided to us by people in the market."
Lazerson said that Moody's could not comment on that information without reviewing it.
"It's hard to repond to unnamed market studies," she said, adding that Moody's received high marks in 1995 and 1996 independent studies comparing rating agencies.
--Karen Pierog, 312-408-8647
